title: Formulae and Chemical Equations
description: Deduce molecular, empirical and ionic formulae from particles and charges; construct word, symbol and ionic equations with balanced atoms, charge and state symbols for Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620.

notes.heading: What a Formula Tells You
notes.body:
📌 A chemical formula uses element symbols and subscripts to show the relative numbers of atoms or ions. A **molecular formula** gives the actual number and type of each atom in one molecule.

🔑 Reading subscripts and brackets
• H₂O contains 2 H atoms and 1 O atom.
• CO₂ contains 1 C atom and 2 O atoms.
• Ca(OH)₂ contains 1 Ca, 2 O and 2 H atoms: the subscript 2 multiplies everything inside the brackets.
• 2NH₃ means two ammonia molecules, giving 2 N and 6 H atoms in total.

💡 Worked Example
A model contains one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms joined together. Its molecular formula is CH₄, not C₄H.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Changing subscripts when balancing an equation. H₂O is water; H₄O₂ is not an alternative way to write two water molecules—use 2H₂O.

📎 Key Points to Remember
Subscripts belong to a formula; coefficients in front show numbers of complete particles.

notes.heading: Molecular and Empirical Formulae
notes.body:
📌 The **empirical formula** is the simplest whole-number ratio of the different atoms or ions in a compound. The molecular formula may be the same as, or a whole-number multiple of, the empirical formula.

🔑 Reducing a ratio
Divide every subscript by their largest common factor. C₂H₄ has ratio 2:4 = 1:2, so its empirical formula is CH₂. H₂O has ratio 2:1, which cannot be reduced, so its empirical formula is also H₂O.

💡 Worked Example
A molecule has formula C₃H₆. Divide both subscripts by 3: the empirical formula is CH₂. Different molecules such as C₂H₄ and C₃H₆ can therefore share an empirical formula.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing an empirical formula with fractional or decimal subscripts. It must use the simplest whole-number ratio.

📎 Key Points to Remember
Molecular = actual atom counts; empirical = simplest ratio. Ionic compounds are normally written using their simplest ratio.

notes.heading: Ionic Formulae: Balance the Charges
notes.body:
📌 An ionic compound has no overall charge. Combine positive and negative ions in a ratio whose total charges cancel.

🔑 The charge-balance method
1. Write each ion and its charge.
2. Choose numbers of ions so positive charge = negative charge.
3. Write the simplest ratio, using brackets around a polyatomic ion if more than one is needed.

💡 Worked Examples
• Mg²⁺ with Cl⁻: MgCl₂, because +2 + 2(−1) = 0.
• Al³⁺ with O²⁻: Al₂O₃, because 2(+3) + 3(−2) = 0.
• Ca²⁺ with NO₃⁻: Ca(NO₃)₂.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Copying the charges as subscripts without simplifying. Ca²⁺ and O²⁻ give CaO, not Ca₂O₂, because the 1:1 ratio already balances.

📎 Key Points to Remember
Check both atom ratio and total charge. Never leave a charge on the final neutral formula.

illustration.alt: Charge-balance examples show one magnesium ion with two chloride ions, two aluminium ions with three oxide ions, and one calcium ion with two nitrate ions, each giving zero total charge.
illustration.caption: Choose the simplest ion ratio that makes total positive and negative charge equal.

notes.heading: Word and Symbol Equations
notes.body:
📌 A word equation names reactants and products; a symbol equation uses their correct formulae. Reactants go on the left and products on the right, separated by an arrow.

🔑 Building the equation
For magnesium burning in oxygen: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide, then Mg + O₂ → MgO, then balance to 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.

🔑 State symbols
Use (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas and (aq) aqueous—dissolved in water. Add them after the formula, not as subscripts.

💡 Worked Example
Calcium carbonate solid decomposes into calcium oxide solid and carbon dioxide gas: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g).

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing oxygen as O instead of O₂ when it is a gaseous element. Hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen and the halogens are diatomic in their uncombined states.

📎 Key Points to Remember
Correct formulae first, coefficients second, state symbols last.

notes.heading: Balancing Without Changing Substances
notes.body:
📌 Atoms are conserved in a chemical reaction. Balance by changing only coefficients—the numbers in front of complete formulae.

🔑 A reliable method
1. Count each element on both sides.
2. Balance one element at a time, leaving elements that appear in only one reactant and one product until useful.
3. Reduce coefficients if they share a common factor.
4. Recount every atom.

💡 Worked Example
CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O. Carbon is balanced. Four H atoms need 2H₂O; the products then contain four O atoms, so use 2O₂:
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Changing CO₂ to CO₄ to balance oxygen. That creates a different substance and invalidates the equation.

📎 Key Points to Remember
The final equation must have the same number of every element on each side and the smallest whole-number coefficients.

notes.heading: Ionic Equations and Spectator Ions
notes.body:
📌 An ionic equation shows only the particles that change. Ions present unchanged on both sides are **spectator ions** and are cancelled.

🔑 Constructing one
1. Write the balanced full equation.
2. Split soluble ionic compounds into aqueous ions; keep solids, liquids, gases and molecules intact.
3. Cancel spectators.
4. Balance atoms AND total charge, with state symbols.

💡 Worked Example
AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq) becomes Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s). Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectators.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Splitting an insoluble precipitate such as AgCl(s) into ions. A solid remains together in the ionic equation.

📎 Key Points to Remember
A correct ionic equation is balanced in both atom counts and electrical charge.

notes.heading: Deducing an Equation from Information
notes.body:
📌 Extended questions may describe an unfamiliar reaction. Use names, ion charges, observations and conservation to deduce the equation rather than memorising it.

🔑 The sequence
Identify every reactant and product → write correct formulae → add states from the description → balance atoms → for an ionic equation, remove spectators and check charge.

💡 Worked Example
Aqueous barium chloride reacts with aqueous sodium sulfate to form a white barium sulfate precipitate and aqueous sodium chloride. The ionic equation is Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s). The Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions remain unchanged.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting the 2+ charge on barium or writing sulfate as SO₄⁻. Total charge on the left is 2+ + 2− = 0, matching the neutral solid.

📎 Key Points to Remember
Treat unfamiliar equations as a deduction problem: formula, states, atoms, charge.

flashcards.definition: The actual number and type of each atom in one molecule of a compound.
flashcards.example: C₂H₄ has two carbon atoms and four hydrogen atoms per molecule.

flashcards.definition: The simplest whole-number ratio of the different atoms or ions in a compound.
flashcards.example: C₂H₄ and C₃H₆ both have empirical formula CH₂.

flashcards.definition: A subscript outside brackets multiplies every atom inside the brackets.
flashcards.example: Ca(OH)₂ contains one Ca, two O and two H atoms.

flashcards.definition: Use the simplest ion ratio that makes total positive and negative charges cancel.
flashcards.example: Al³⁺ and O²⁻ combine as Al₂O₃.

flashcards.definition: Use brackets when more than one of a polyatomic ion appears in a formula.
flashcards.example: Ca²⁺ with NO₃⁻ gives Ca(NO₃)₂, not CaNO₃₂.

flashcards.definition: A number before a formula that multiplies the complete particle; used to balance equations.
flashcards.example: 3H₂ represents six hydrogen atoms in three hydrogen molecules.

flashcards.definition: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas and (aq) aqueous or dissolved in water.
flashcards.example: NaCl(aq) is dissolved sodium chloride; AgCl(s) is a solid precipitate.

flashcards.definition: A balanced equation has equal numbers of each type of atom on both sides.
flashcards.example: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O balances C, H and O.

flashcards.definition: Change coefficients only, never the subscripts within a correct chemical formula.
flashcards.example: Balance hydrogen with 2H₂O, not by changing water to H₄O.

flashcards.definition: An aqueous ion that remains unchanged on both sides and is omitted from the ionic equation.
flashcards.example: Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectators when Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ form AgCl(s).

flashcards.definition: Include the aqueous ions that combine and the insoluble solid formed, balancing atoms and charge.
H₂, N₂, O₂ and the halogens exist as diatomic molecules when uncombined.
flashcards.example: Oxygen gas is written O₂(g), not O(g).

questions.stem: How many oxygen atoms are represented by 3Ca(NO₃)₂?
questions.explanation: Each NO₃ group has 3 O atoms and there are 2 groups per formula unit, giving 6. The coefficient 3 gives 3 × 6 = 18 oxygen atoms.

questions.stem: What is the empirical formula of C₄H₈?
questions.explanation: The atom ratio 4:8 simplifies to 1:2 by dividing by 4, so the empirical formula is CH₂.

questions.stem: Which formula results from Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions?
questions.explanation: Two Cl⁻ ions balance one Mg²⁺ ion, giving MgCl₂ with zero total charge.

questions.stem: Which state symbol means dissolved in water?
questions.explanation: (aq) means aqueous: dissolved in water. (l) is a pure liquid, not a solution.

questions.stem: What is the formula of aluminium oxide, formed from Al³⁺ and O²⁻?
questions.explanation: Two Al³⁺ ions give +6 and three O²⁻ ions give −6, so the neutral formula is Al₂O₃.

questions.stem: Which equation is correctly balanced for methane combustion?
questions.explanation: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O has 1 C, 4 H and 4 O atoms on both sides.

questions.stem: What is the empirical formula of C₆H₁₂O₆?
questions.explanation: All three subscripts divide by 6, giving the simplest whole-number ratio C:H:O = 1:2:1, or CH₂O.

questions.stem: Which formula correctly combines Ca²⁺ with NO₃⁻?
questions.explanation: Two nitrate ions balance one calcium ion. Brackets are essential: Ca(NO₃)₂ contains two complete NO₃ groups.

questions.stem: In the reaction AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq), which are spectator ions?
questions.explanation: Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ remain aqueous and unchanged. Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ combine to form solid AgCl.

questions.stem: Which ionic equation represents the formation of barium sulfate precipitate?
questions.explanation: Aqueous Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions combine to form insoluble BaSO₄(s). Charges balance to zero and the precipitate is solid.

questions.stem: A model of one molecule contains 2 nitrogen atoms and 4 oxygen atoms. What are its molecular and empirical formulae?
questions.explanation: The actual counts give N₂O₄. Dividing both subscripts by 2 gives the empirical formula NO₂.

questions.stem: Which change correctly balances N₂ + H₂ → NH₃?
choices: Change N₂ to N and H₂ to H
questions.explanation: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ has 2 N and 6 H atoms on each side. Subscripts must not be altered.

questions.stem: Which full equation follows from the ionic equation H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l)?
questions.explanation: In HCl + NaOH, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectators, leaving H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O. The other reactions include additional changes.

questions.stem: Which equation has balanced atoms AND balanced charge?
questions.explanation: Fe²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₂(s) balances Fe, O and H and has zero net charge on both sides.

questions.stem: Which equation correctly represents hydrogen burning in oxygen?
questions.explanation: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O conserves 4 H and 2 O atoms and uses the correct diatomic reactant formulae.
